curve-analysis__ca-concavity__mcq.prompt: A curve has f′ < 0 and f″ > 0. What is it doing?

options.label: Falling, but the fall is levelling off — bending back upward.
options.feedback: Right. The slope is negative and INCREASING (toward zero), which is exactly what a car braking to a stop looks like.

options.label: Rising and speeding up.
options.feedback: Rising needs f′ > 0. This curve is going down.

options.label: Falling faster and faster.
options.feedback: That would be f″ < 0 — a negative slope getting MORE negative. Here f″ is positive, so the slope is rising toward zero.

options.label: That combination is impossible.
options.feedback: It is extremely common: any curve approaching a minimum from the left is falling and concave up.

curve-analysis__ca-critical-point__mcq.prompt: Why does the definition include 'f′ does not exist' as well as 'f′ = 0'?

options.label: Because |x| has a minimum at its corner, where f′ does not exist at all.
options.feedback: Right — a definition that said only 'f′ = 0' would miss that minimum entirely. Extrema can hide at corners.

options.label: For completeness; it never actually happens.
options.feedback: It happens constantly — every corner, cusp and vertical tangent. And |x| puts a genuine minimum at one.

options.label: Because f′ = 0 is hard to solve.
options.feedback: Difficulty is not the reason. The reason is that some extrema sit at points where no tangent exists.

options.label: Because a vertical tangent is a maximum.
options.feedback: A vertical tangent might be a maximum, a minimum, or neither — which is exactly why it must be treated as a SUSPECT rather than ignored.

curve-analysis__ca-evt__mcq.prompt: Why does f(x) = x on the OPEN interval (0, 1) have no maximum?

options.label: It climbs all the way to 1 but never reaches it — the endpoint is not included.
options.feedback: Right, and that is precisely why the EVT insists on a CLOSED interval. Without the ends, the maximum can escape.

options.label: Because f′ is never zero.
options.feedback: True, but not the reason — on the CLOSED interval [0, 1] the same function has a maximum of 1, at an endpoint, with f′ still never zero.

options.label: Because it is not continuous.
options.feedback: f(x) = x is continuous everywhere. The failure is in the interval, not the function.

options.label: It does have one: 1.
options.feedback: 1 is not IN the open interval, so f never attains it. There is a supremum, but no maximum.

curve-analysis__ca-first-derivative-test.prompt: f′ is positive on (−∞, −2), negative on (−2, 2), positive on (2, ∞). Where is f DECREASING?

options.label: On (−2, 2) — the interval where f′ is negative.
options.feedback: Right. Decreasing is a statement about the SIGN of f′, and nothing else.

options.label: On (−∞, −2).
options.feedback: f′ is POSITIVE there, so f is climbing, not falling.

options.label: At x = −2 and x = 2.
options.feedback: At those points f′ = 0, so f is momentarily flat — neither rising nor falling. Decreasing happens on the interval BETWEEN them.

options.label: Nowhere — f′ is a parabola opening upward.
options.feedback: An upward parabola dips BELOW the axis between its roots, and that dip is exactly where f falls.

curve-analysis__ca-first-derivative-test.prompt: f(x) = x³ − 12x, with f′ positive, then negative, then positive. Find the local MAXIMUM value of f.

commonErrors.feedback: That is WHERE the maximum occurs. The question asks for its VALUE: f(−2) = −8 + 24 = 16.
That is f(2), the local MINIMUM. The maximum is at x = −2, where f = 16.
That is where the minimum occurs. The maximum is at x = −2, and its value is 16.

curve-analysis__ca-first-derivative-test.fallbackFeedback: f′ goes + → − at x = −2, so f(−2) = −8 + 24 = 16 is a local maximum.

curve-analysis__ca-first-derivative-test.prompt: f(x) = x⁴ − 4x³. How many local EXTREMA does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: There are two critical points, but only ONE is an extremum. At x = 0 the derivative touches zero without changing sign — a saddle.
There is one: at x = 3, f′ crosses from negative to positive, so f falls into it and climbs out. A minimum.
f′ = 4x²(x − 3) has only two distinct roots, and only one of them is a sign change.

curve-analysis__ca-first-derivative-test.fallbackFeedback: f′ = 4x²(x−3) goes −, −, +: only x = 3 is a sign change, so there is exactly one extremum (a minimum).

curve-analysis__ca-first-derivative-test.prompt: f(x) = x⁴ − 4x³, so f′(x) = 4x²(x − 3). Set the signs of f′ — and watch the double root.
curve-analysis__ca-first-derivative-test.successFeedback: − − +. The double root at 0 does NOT flip the sign, so f′ is negative on both sides of it: f is falling into x = 0 and still falling out. It is a critical point and it is NOT an extremum — a saddle. Only x = 3, where f′ genuinely crosses, is a minimum. The bounce-versus-cross rule has just become a statement about peaks and valleys.
curve-analysis__ca-first-derivative-test.crossFeedback: The root at 3 is single, so f′ must change sign there.
curve-analysis__ca-first-derivative-test.bounceFeedback: You flipped the sign across x = 0, but that root of f′ is DOUBLE. f′ touches zero and returns to the side it came from — so f keeps falling, and there is no extremum.

curve-analysis__ca-inflection__mcq.prompt: What makes x = c an inflection point?

options.label: f″ CHANGES SIGN at c — the bend switches direction.
options.feedback: Right. f″(c) = 0 is a suspect; the sign change is the conviction. It is exactly the same discipline as before, one level up.

options.label: f″(c) = 0.
options.feedback: Necessary but not sufficient — and x⁴ is the counterexample: f″ = 12x² is zero at 0 but never changes sign, so the curve stays concave up throughout.

options.label: f′(c) = 0.
options.feedback: That is a critical point, which is about rising and falling. An inflection is about BENDING.

options.label: The curve crosses the x-axis at c.
options.feedback: Crossing the axis is about the sign of f, which has nothing to do with concavity.

curve-analysis__ca-inflection__mcq.prompt: f(x) = x⁴ has f″(0) = 0. Is x = 0 an inflection point?

options.label: No — f″ = 12x² is positive on BOTH sides, so the bend never changes.
options.feedback: Right. It is the x³ trap wearing a different hat: a zero of f″ with no sign change is not an inflection.

options.label: Yes, because f″ = 0 there.
options.feedback: f″ = 0 is a suspect, not a conviction — the very lesson this course opened with, now applied one derivative further up.

options.label: Yes, because x = 0 is a minimum.
options.feedback: It IS a minimum, but that is a fact about f′, not about the bend. The curve is concave up on both sides.

options.label: Only if f is also zero there.
options.feedback: The value of f is irrelevant to concavity. Only the sign of f″ matters.

curve-analysis__ca-inflection__numeric.prompt: f(x) = x⁴ − 4x³. How many inflection points does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: f″ = 12x(x − 2) has TWO single roots, at 0 and 2, and the sign changes at both.
f″ certainly changes sign — it is an upward parabola with two distinct roots, so it dips negative between them.
A quadratic f″ has at most two roots, and here it has exactly two.

curve-analysis__ca-inflection__numeric.fallbackFeedback: f″ = 12x(x − 2): two single roots, two sign changes, two inflection points.

curve-analysis__ca-mvt-consequences__mcq.prompt: f′(x) = 0 for every x. What follows, and why?

options.label: f is constant — the MVT forces f(x₂) − f(x₁) = 0·(x₂ − x₁) = 0 for any two points.
options.feedback: Right, and this is what finally JUSTIFIES the + C: if F′ = G′ then (F − G)′ = 0, so F − G is constant.

options.label: f is zero.
options.feedback: f(x) = 7 has zero derivative and is nowhere near zero. Zero SLOPE, not zero value.

options.label: f is increasing very slowly.
options.feedback: Not at all — it does not increase. The MVT shows f(x₂) equals f(x₁) exactly, for every pair.

options.label: Nothing without more information.
options.feedback: The MVT needs nothing more. Two points and a zero derivative are enough to force equality.

curve-analysis__ca-mvt-consequences__mcq.prompt: Why is every antiderivative of f of the form F + C, with no exceptions?

options.label: Two antiderivatives have the same derivative, so their difference has derivative 0 — and the MVT says that makes it constant.
options.feedback: Right. Without the MVT you could not rule out some stranger relationship, and the + C would be a hope rather than a theorem.

options.label: By definition.
options.feedback: The definition says F′ = f. It does not, by itself, say that ALL such F differ by a constant — that is a theorem, and the MVT proves it.

options.label: Because constants have zero derivative.
options.feedback: That shows F + C IS an antiderivative. The harder direction — that there are no OTHERS — is what needs the MVT.

options.label: It is an assumption we make.
options.feedback: It is proved, not assumed. That is the difference the MVT makes.

curve-analysis__ca-optimisation-applied_.prompt: 100 m of fence, three sides only (the wall is the fourth). Which area formula is right?

options.label: A = x(100 − 2x)
options.feedback: Right — two depths and one width use the fence, so y = 100 − 2x.

options.label: A = x(50 − x)
options.feedback: That is the four-sided pen, where 2x + 2y = 100 gives y = 50 − x. The wall means you only fence THREE sides, so more fence is left for the width.

options.label: A = x(100 − x)
options.feedback: That uses only ONE depth. There are two sides of length x, so the fence they consume is 2x.

options.label: A = 100x
options.feedback: That ignores the constraint entirely — it says the width is 100 no matter how deep the pen is, which would need infinite fence.

curve-analysis__ca-optimisation-applied_.prompt: A profit function P(x) has P′(x) > 0 for every x in the allowed range [0, 40]. Where is the maximum profit?

options.label: At x = 40 — the right endpoint. Profit is still climbing when the range runs out.
options.feedback: Right, and there is no critical point at all: the tangent is never flat. This is why the endpoints must ALWAYS be checked.

options.label: There is no maximum, since P′ is never zero.
options.feedback: On a CLOSED interval the EVT guarantees a maximum. It just does not have to be at a critical point — here it is at the edge.

options.label: At x = 0.
options.feedback: That is where profit is SMALLEST: the function climbs from there all the way to 40.

options.label: Somewhere in the middle.
options.feedback: An interior maximum needs f′ to change sign. Here f′ is positive throughout — the curve climbs right up to the edge.

curve-analysis__ca-optimisation-applied_.prompt: Find the maximum area of the pen, in square metres.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 50 × 50 — a square pen, which would need 150 m of fence for three sides. You only have 100.
That is 25², the depth squared. The width is 100 − 50 = 50, so the area is 25 × 50 = 1250.
That is the width y at the optimum. Multiply by the depth 25 to get the area.

curve-analysis__ca-optimisation-applied_.prompt: Two numbers add to 20. What is the SMALLEST possible sum of their squares?

commonErrors.feedback: That is 20² — what you get if one number is 0 and the other is 20. That is an ENDPOINT, and it is the maximum, not the minimum.
That is 10², the square of one number. The sum of BOTH squares is 100 + 100 = 200.
That is the value of x at the optimum. The sum of squares there is 200.

curve-analysis__ca-optimisation-setup__d.prompt: Put an optimisation problem in the right order.

items.label: Write a formula for the quantity to be optimised
Differentiate, and compare critical points with the endpoints
Use the constraint to reduce it to ONE variable

misorderFeedback.feedback: You cannot differentiate a formula with two variables in it. Eliminate one first.
You cannot state the domain of a formula you have not written yet.

curve-analysis__ca-optimisation-setup__d.missFeedback: Formula, then constraint, then domain, then calculus.
curve-analysis__ca-optimisation-setup__d.successFeedback: Formula, constraint, domain, calculus. Three translation steps and one differentiation.

curve-analysis__ca-read-f-prime__matchPa.prompt: You are looking at a graph of f′. Match each feature to what it says about f.

pairErrors.feedback: f′ being POSITIVE means f is climbing. An extremum needs f′ to be ZERO, which happens at a crossing.
f′ RISING is a statement about the bend of f (concave up), not about its direction. Direction comes from the SIGN of f′, not its slope.

curve-analysis__ca-read-f-prime__matchPa.missFeedback: Height of f′ = slope of f. Slope of f′ = bend of f.
curve-analysis__ca-read-f-prime__matchPa.successFeedback: Height gives direction; slope gives bend; a crossing gives an extremum. That table is the whole skill.

curve-analysis__ca-read-f-prime__mcq.prompt: The graph of f′ crosses the axis from ABOVE to BELOW at x = 2. What is at x = 2 on the graph of f?

options.label: A local maximum of f.
options.feedback: Right — f was rising (f′ > 0), then falls (f′ < 0). It turned over at x = 2.

options.label: A zero of f.
options.feedback: That is what the graph would mean if it were f. But it is f′ — its zero is a FLAT SPOT of f, not a root.

options.label: An inflection point of f.
options.feedback: Inflections come from where f′ has an extremum (its own peak or valley), not where f′ crosses zero.

options.label: A local minimum of f.
options.feedback: That would need f′ to cross from BELOW to ABOVE. Here it goes the other way, so f climbs then falls.

curve-analysis__ca-read-f-prime__mcq.prompt: The graph of f′ has a MAXIMUM at x = 1 (it peaks and comes back down, staying positive). What is at x = 1 on f?

options.label: An inflection point — and the steepest climb of f.
options.feedback: Right. f′ peaking means f″ = 0 with a sign change: the bend flips, and f is climbing as fast as it ever does.

options.label: A maximum of f.
options.feedback: f′ is still POSITIVE at its own peak, so f is still climbing. A maximum of f needs f′ to reach ZERO.

options.label: A minimum of f.
options.feedback: f is rising throughout (f′ > 0). It cannot have a minimum in the middle of a climb.

options.label: A zero of f.
options.feedback: The graph shown is f′, and its shape says nothing about where f crosses the axis.

curve-analysis__ca-read-f-prime__numeric.prompt: A graph of f′ touches the axis at x = 1 without crossing, and crosses it at x = 4. How many EXTREMA does f have?

commonErrors.feedback: A touch is not a crossing. At x = 1 the derivative returns to the side it came from, so f does not turn — that is a saddle.
There is one: at x = 4, f′ genuinely changes sign, so f turns round.
Only two features are described, and only one of them is a sign change.

curve-analysis__ca-read-f-prime__numeric.fallbackFeedback: Only the crossing at x = 4 changes the sign of f′, so f has exactly one extremum.

curve-analysis__ca-rolle__mcq.prompt: f(x) = |x| − 1 on [−1, 1] has f(−1) = f(1) = 0, yet f′ is never zero. Which hypothesis fails?

options.label: Differentiability — there is a corner at x = 0.
options.feedback: Right, and it is the whole point: without differentiability the curve can turn round at a corner, where there is no tangent to be flat.

options.label: Continuity.
options.feedback: |x| − 1 is perfectly continuous — you can draw it without lifting the pen. The failure is in the SLOPE, not the value.

options.label: f(a) = f(b).
options.feedback: Both ends are 0, so that hypothesis holds. Something else has broken.

options.label: None — Rolle is simply false.
options.feedback: Rolle is a theorem, and theorems do not fail. What fails is a hypothesis — differentiability, at the corner.

curve-analysis__ca-second-derivative-tes.prompt: f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) = 0. What can you conclude?

options.label: Nothing — use the sign chart of f′ instead.
options.feedback: Right. x⁴, −x⁴ and x³ all give this result and are a minimum, a maximum and a saddle respectively.

options.label: It is an inflection point.
options.feedback: It might be — but x⁴ has f″(0) = 0 and is a MINIMUM, with no inflection at all. f″ = 0 needs a sign change to mean anything.

options.label: It is a saddle.
options.feedback: x⁴ has f′(0) = f″(0) = 0 and is a genuine minimum. The test simply cannot see the difference.

options.label: It is a minimum.
options.feedback: −x⁴ has exactly the same test values and is a maximum. The result is inconclusive, which is a real answer and not a failure.

curve-analysis__ca-second-derivative-tes.prompt: f has a critical point at a CORNER, where f′ does not exist. Which test can classify it?

options.label: The first-derivative test — look at the sign of f′ on either side.
options.feedback: Right. |x| is the standard case: f′ is −1 to the left and +1 to the right, so it is a minimum, and f″ never enters the argument.

options.label: The second-derivative test.
options.feedback: If f′ does not exist at the point, f″ certainly does not. The test cannot even be stated there.

options.label: Neither — corners cannot be classified.
options.feedback: They can, easily: the sign of f′ on either side of the corner tells you everything.

options.label: Both work equally well.
options.feedback: The second-derivative test needs f″(c) to exist, and at a corner it does not.

curve-analysis__ca-three-charts__matchPa.prompt: Match each pair of signs to what the curve is doing.

pairErrors.feedback: f″ < 0 means the slope is SHRINKING, so the climb is easing off rather than steepening.
f′ < 0 means the curve is going DOWN, not climbing.

curve-analysis__ca-three-charts__matchPa.missFeedback: The sign of f′ says up or down. The sign of f″ says whether that is intensifying or easing.
curve-analysis__ca-three-charts__matchPa.successFeedback: Direction from f′, and whether it is intensifying from f″. Four combinations, and every point on every curve is one of them.

curve-analysis__ca-three-charts__mcq.prompt: For f = x⁴ − 4x³, x = 0 is a critical point with no sign change in f′, AND a sign change in f″. What is it?

options.label: A saddle AND an inflection point — the two charts describe different things.
options.feedback: Right. f′ says the curve does not turn; f″ says the bend does. Both are true at once, and neither implies the other.

options.label: A minimum.
options.feedback: A minimum needs f′ to change from negative to positive. Here f′ is negative on both sides — the curve is falling through the point.

options.label: Only an inflection — it cannot be a critical point too.
options.feedback: It can, and it is: f′(0) = 0, which is exactly what a critical point means. The two labels are independent.

options.label: Nothing special.
options.feedback: Both derivatives vanish there and one changes sign. That is a great deal of structure for one point.

curve-analysis__ca-three-charts__mcq.prompt: On an interval, f′ > 0 and f″ < 0. What is the curve doing, and what is it approaching?

options.label: Rising, but levelling off — heading toward a maximum.
options.feedback: Right. Positive slope, decreasing slope: the climb is running out of steam, which is what the approach to a peak looks like.

options.label: Rising and accelerating.
options.feedback: That needs f″ > 0 — the slope getting steeper. Here the slope is shrinking.

options.label: Falling and levelling off.
options.feedback: Falling needs f′ < 0. This curve is going UP; it is just going up more and more gently.

options.label: At a maximum already.
options.feedback: At the maximum f′ would be 0. It is still positive, so the peak has not arrived yet.

curve-analysis__ca-three-charts__numeric.prompt: f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 5. How many inflection points does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: Two is the number of CRITICAL points (0 and 4). Inflections come from f″ = 6x − 12, which has a single root at x = 2.
f″ = 6x − 12 does change sign — negative for x < 2 and positive after. That is one inflection.
A linear f″ can change sign at most once.

curve-analysis__ca-three-charts__numeric.fallbackFeedback: f″ = 6(x − 2): one root, one sign change, one inflection point.

derivative-rules__dr-chain-nested__mcq.prompt: How many factors will the derivative of √((2x + 1)³) have?

options.label: Three — one for the root, one for the cube, one for the bracket.
options.feedback: Right. Every layer contributes exactly one factor, and the innermost is the one people drop.

options.label: Two — a chain rule only ever has two.
options.feedback: The chain rule has two factors PER APPLICATION, and here it is applied twice. Layers, not applications, is the count that matters.

options.label: One — you can simplify it away.
options.feedback: It does simplify to (2x+1)^(3/2), which is still a chain: outer power, inner bracket. You never escape the inside.

options.label: Four.
options.feedback: Count the layers: root, cube, linear. Three layers, three factors.

commonErrors.feedback: The second term vanishes at x = 0 (because of the factor x), but the FIRST term does not: (2·0+1)³ = 1.
That is the inner factor 6(2x+1)² at x = 0 — but it is multiplied by x, which is 0. The surviving term is (2x+1)³ = 1.
Check the product rule: 1·(2x+1)³ + x·6(2x+1)². At x = 0 that is 1 + 0.

derivative-rules__dr-chain-rule__mcq.prompt: For f(x) = (3x + 1)⁵, what is the derivative?

options.label: 15(3x + 1)⁴
options.feedback: Right — 5(3x+1)⁴ from the outside, times 3 from the inside. The inner derivative is the part everyone forgets.

options.label: 5(3x + 1)⁴
options.feedback: The outside is right, but you have not paid for the inside. The bracket changes 3 times as fast as x does, so the whole thing must be multiplied by 3.

options.label: 5(3)⁴
options.feedback: The inside must stay intact inside the bracket. The power rule acts on the WHOLE bracket, not on the 3 alone.

options.label: 15(3x + 1)⁵
options.feedback: The power must drop by one: (3x+1)⁴, not ⁵. The 15 is right, though.

derivative-rules__dr-critical-point__num.prompt: f(x) = x³ − 12x has f′(x) = 3x² − 12. How many critical points does f have?

commonErrors.feedback: 3x² − 12 = 0 gives x² = 4, and a square equals 4 at TWO values: x = 2 and x = −2.
3x² − 12 does hit zero — at x = ±2. A derivative that is a parabola crosses the axis twice here.
A quadratic derivative has at most two zeros. 3x² = 12 gives exactly two.

derivative-rules__dr-derivative-function.prompt: You traced f′ for f(x) = x². What kind of object is f′?

options.label: A function — one slope for each input, here f′(x) = 2x.
options.feedback: Right. That is the promotion: from a slope AT a point to a slope FUNCTION over the whole domain.

options.label: A number — the slope of the curve.
options.feedback: A curve has no single slope; it has a different one at every point. That is precisely why the derivative must be a function.

options.label: The tangent line at a point.
options.feedback: The tangent is a LINE at one x. f′ is the rule that tells you the slope of that line for every x at once.

options.label: The limit of a single secant.
options.feedback: That is f′ at ONE point — the precalculus version. Doing it at every point is what turns it into a function.

commonErrors.feedback: That is f(−4), the HEIGHT of the curve. The derivative reports the SLOPE, which is 2(−4) = −8. A curve can be high and falling at the same time.
The sign is wrong. f′(x) = 2x, and 2 × (−4) is −8: on the left arm of the parabola the curve is going DOWN.
That is x itself. The rule doubles it: f′(−4) = 2(−4) = −8.

derivative-rules__dr-derivative-function.fallbackFeedback: f′(x) = 2x, so f′(−4) = −8 — the curve is falling steeply there.

derivative-rules__dr-differentiability__.prompt: At which of these does f′ FAIL to exist?

items.label: A corner, like |x| at 0
items.feedback: Two one-sided slopes that disagree — the limit has no single value.

items.label: A jump discontinuity
items.feedback: If f is not even continuous, no tangent can exist. Differentiable ⇒ continuous, so not-continuous ⇒ not-differentiable.

items.label: A vertical tangent, like ∛x at 0
items.feedback: The slope runs off to infinity, and infinity is not a number. The tangent exists as a LINE but the derivative does not exist as a VALUE.

items.label: A smooth minimum, like x² at 0
items.feedback: Perfectly differentiable: f′(0) = 0. A flat tangent is still a tangent.

derivative-rules__dr-differentiability__.missFeedback: Ask whether the limit [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h settles on ONE finite number.
derivative-rules__dr-differentiability__.successFeedback: Corners, cusps, vertical tangents and discontinuities all break the limit. A flat tangent breaks nothing.

derivative-rules__dr-differentiability__.prompt: |x| is continuous at x = 0 but has no derivative there. What does that tell you?

options.label: Continuity is necessary for differentiability, but not sufficient.
options.feedback: Right, and the implication runs one way only: differentiable ⇒ continuous, never the reverse.

options.label: Continuity and differentiability are the same thing.
options.feedback: |x| is the standing refutation: continuous everywhere, differentiable everywhere except one point.

options.label: |x| must be discontinuous at 0.
options.feedback: It is not — the two halves meet at (0, 0) with no gap and no jump. The failure is in the SLOPE, not the value.

options.label: The derivative is 0 at the corner, by symmetry.
options.feedback: Symmetry is a tempting argument and it is wrong: the one-sided slopes are −1 and +1, and a limit with two answers has none.

derivative-rules__dr-differentiability__.prompt: A function has a jump at x = −2, a corner at x = 0, a vertical tangent at x = 3, and a smooth minimum at x = 5. At how many of these four points does f′ FAIL to exist?

commonErrors.feedback: The smooth minimum is fine — a horizontal tangent is still a tangent, and f′ = 0 there. Only the first three break.
All three of the jump, the corner and the vertical tangent break the limit. Only the smooth minimum survives.
Each of the jump, the corner and the vertical tangent kills the limit in its own way — that is three failures.

derivative-rules__dr-differentiability__.fallbackFeedback: Jump, corner and vertical tangent: three failures. The smooth minimum has f′ = 0, which exists.

commonErrors.feedback: The derivative of eˣ is eˣ, not 0 — and e⁰ = 1. It is the only function that survives differentiation unchanged.
That is e¹, the value at x = 1. At x = 0 the height (and so the slope) is e⁰ = 1.
e ≈ 2.718, but you want e⁰, which is 1.

derivative-rules__dr-flat-not-turning__m.prompt: For f(x) = x³, f′(0) = 0. Does f have a peak or a valley at x = 0?

options.label: Neither — it flattens and keeps climbing. f′ never changes sign.
options.feedback: Right. A turning point needs f′ to change SIGN, not merely to touch zero. This is exactly the bounce-versus-cross idea from sign charts, arriving in calculus.

options.label: A valley, because f′ = 0.
options.feedback: f′ = 0 is necessary for a turning point but nowhere near sufficient. Look at the curve: it never turns.

options.label: A peak, because the tangent is horizontal.
options.feedback: Horizontal tangents happen at peaks, at valleys, AND at flat pauses like this one. The tangent alone cannot tell you which.

options.label: Impossible to say without f″.
options.feedback: You can already say it from f′ alone: f′ = 3x² is positive either side of 0, so the curve rises into the point and rises out of it.

derivative-rules__dr-implicit-practice__.prompt: On x² + y² = 25, why does dy/dx = −x/y depend on y as well as x?

options.label: Because the curve has two points above most x-values, with opposite slopes — and only y can distinguish them.
options.feedback: Right. At (3, 4) the slope is −3/4 and at (3, −4) it is +3/4. A formula in x alone would have to choose one and be wrong about the other.

options.label: Because we made a mistake and failed to eliminate y.
options.feedback: Nothing went wrong. The dependence on y is information, not residue — it is what lets one formula serve the whole curve.

options.label: Because the circle is not a function.
options.feedback: True, and that is WHY implicit differentiation exists — but the question is what the y in the answer is doing, and it is telling the two branches apart.

options.label: It does not really — you can always substitute y = √(25 − x²).
options.feedback: You can, on the top half. Then you need a second formula for the bottom half. The implicit answer covers both at once.

derivative-rules__dr-implicit__mcq.prompt: Differentiating y² with respect to x gives what?

options.label: 2y·(dy/dx)
options.feedback: Right — y is a function of x, so the chain rule charges you its derivative. That is the whole trick of implicit differentiation.

options.label: 2y
options.feedback: That would be right if you were differentiating with respect to y. With respect to x, the chain rule adds a factor of dy/dx.

options.label: 2x
options.feedback: There is no x in y². The variable being squared is y.

options.label: 0, because y is not x.
options.feedback: y is not a constant — it changes as x changes, which is exactly why it has a derivative dy/dx.

derivative-rules__dr-implicit__numeric.prompt: x² + y² = 25. Find dy/dx at the point (3, 4), as a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: The sign is wrong. 2x + 2y·y′ = 0 gives y′ = −x/y, and at (3, 4) that is −3/4: the circle is FALLING there, in the upper right quadrant.
That is 4/3 — the slope of the RADIUS to that point. The tangent is perpendicular to it, so its slope is the negative reciprocal, −3/4.
Close, but inverted: dy/dx = −x/y = −3/4, not −y/x.

derivative-rules__dr-limit-definition__m.prompt: f(x) = x². Simplify [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h before taking the limit.

options.label: 2x + h
options.feedback: Right — and now h → 0 kills the leftover h, leaving f′(x) = 2x. The division by h is legal precisely because h is not yet zero.

options.label: 2x
options.feedback: That is the answer AFTER the limit. Before it, the h² term leaves a stray h behind: 2x + h.

options.label: 2x + h²
options.feedback: The h² was divided by h, so it comes down to h, not h². Expand carefully: (2xh + h²)/h = 2x + h.
That is what you get if you substitute h = 0 too early — the same 0/0 trap you met in limits. The cancellation must happen first.

derivative-rules__dr-local-linearity__mc.prompt: You magnify a graph at a point and it becomes indistinguishable from a straight line. What have you shown?

options.label: f is differentiable there — locally straight is what having a derivative looks like.
options.feedback: Right, and it is the geometric meaning of the limit: the closer you look, the better the tangent fits.

options.label: f is a straight line.
options.feedback: Only NEAR that point. Zoom back out and it may be a wild curve — local straightness is a local claim.

options.label: f′ = 0 there.
options.feedback: The line you see can have any slope. Locally straight says a tangent EXISTS, not that it is flat.

options.label: Nothing — every graph looks straight up close.
options.feedback: Not so: magnify |x| at its corner and it stays bent at exactly the same angle, no matter how far you zoom.

derivative-rules__dr-sign-of-derivative_.prompt: Match what f is doing to what f′ is doing.

pairErrors.feedback: Falling means f′ is NEGATIVE. The word 'gently' is about size; the word 'falling' is about sign.
f′ = 0 is a flat tangent — the opposite of climbing steeply.

derivative-rules__dr-sign-of-derivative_.missFeedback: Sign of f′ = direction of f. Size of f′ = steepness of f.
derivative-rules__dr-sign-of-derivative_.successFeedback: Direction from the sign, steepness from the size. Height does not enter into it.

derivative-rules__dr-sign-of-derivative_.prompt: f′(x) = 3x² − 12. How many INTEGER values of x have f falling (f′ < 0)?

commonErrors.feedback: That counts −2 and 2 as well, but there f′ = 0 exactly — flat, not falling. The inequality is strict.
Check the endpoints: at x = ±2 the derivative is 0, not negative. Only −1, 0, 1 are strictly inside.
There are three integers strictly between −2 and 2: −1, 0 and 1 — zero counts.

derivative-rules__dr-tangent-line__numer.prompt: f(x) = x², so f′(x) = 2x. Find the y-intercept of the tangent line at x = 3.

commonErrors.feedback: That is f(3), the y-value where the tangent touches the curve — not where it crosses the axis. Run the line back to x = 0: y = 9 + 6(0 − 3) = −9.
That is the slope f′(3), not the intercept. Use it in y − 9 = 6(x − 3) and set x = 0.
The tangent at (3, 9) with slope 6 is nowhere near the origin. y = 6x − 9 crosses at −9.

derivative-rules__dr-tangent-line__numer.fallbackFeedback: y − 9 = 6(x − 3) → y = 6x − 9, so the intercept is −9.

derivative-rules__dr-trig-derivative__mc.prompt: Why does (cos x)′ = −sin x carry a minus sign?

options.label: Just past x = 0 the cosine is falling, so its derivative must be negative — and sin x is positive there.
options.feedback: Right. The minus is forced by the geometry: cosine starts at its peak and goes DOWN, while sine is climbing.

options.label: Because cosine is negative.
options.feedback: cos x is positive for x near 0. The sign in the derivative is about the DIRECTION the curve is heading, not the sign of its height.

options.label: It is a convention.
options.feedback: It is forced. Drop the minus and the formula would claim the cosine is RISING just after its peak, which the graph plainly refutes.

options.label: Because sine and cosine are 90° apart.
options.feedback: They are — and that shift explains why the derivative is the OTHER function, but not why the sign flips. The flip comes from the direction of travel.

derivatives-in-context__dc-choosing-rela.prompt: For the sliding ladder, which quantities VARY with time?

items.label: x, the foot's distance from the wall
items.feedback: It is being dragged outward at 2 ft/s — that IS its rate of change.

items.label: y, the height on the wall
items.feedback: It falls as x grows. Finding its rate is the whole question.

items.label: The ladder's length, 10 ft
items.feedback: A ladder does not stretch. That is why the right-hand side of the differentiated equation is 0.

items.label: The angle with the ground
items.feedback: It certainly changes — the ladder flattens as it slides. It is simply not the variable this problem asks about.

derivatives-in-context__dc-choosing-rela.missFeedback: Ask of each quantity: is it different a second later? If yes, it varies and owes a d/dt.
derivatives-in-context__dc-choosing-rela.successFeedback: Only the ladder's length is fixed. Everything else owes a d/dt — and that is exactly why the equation differentiates to zero.

derivatives-in-context__dc-choosing-rela.prompt: A person walks away from a lamppost; their shadow lengthens. Which relation should you use?

options.label: Similar triangles — the lamp/person/shadow makes two triangles of the same shape.
options.feedback: Right. The person's height over their shadow equals the lamp's height over the whole base — that proportion IS the relation.

options.label: Pythagoras
options.feedback: There is no hypotenuse in question here. The link between the distances is a PROPORTION, not a right-angle relation.

options.label: The area of a triangle
options.feedback: Nothing here has an area, and none is asked for. The quantities are LENGTHS, and they are tied together by similarity of the two triangles.

options.label: The volume of a cone
options.feedback: Nothing here is three-dimensional. That relation belongs to the filling-tank problems.

derivatives-in-context__dc-choosing-rela.prompt: V = (1/3)πr²h, and the cone's shape forces r = h/2. What should you differentiate?

options.label: V = (1/12)πh³ — substitute r = h/2 FIRST, so only h remains.
options.feedback: Right. Differentiating the two-variable version leaves both dr/dt and dh/dt in your answer, and you cannot finish.

options.label: V = (1/3)πr²h, keeping both variables.
options.feedback: Then the product rule gives you an equation with TWO unknown rates. Eliminate r first, using the geometry.

options.label: r = h/2
options.feedback: That is the relation between the variables, not the quantity whose rate you want. Use it to SUBSTITUTE.

options.label: V = πr²h
options.feedback: That is the volume of a CYLINDER. A cone is one third of it — and the relation must be right before any calculus starts.

derivatives-in-context__dc-choosing-rela.prompt: Two cars leave a junction, one north at 40 mph and one east at 30 mph. How fast is the distance between them growing when they are 30 and 40 miles out? (mph)

commonErrors.feedback: That is 30 + 40 — but they are travelling at right angles, so the distance grows along the HYPOTENUSE, not the sum. Use z² = x² + y².
That is 40 − 30. The distance is the hypotenuse, and its rate is (30(30) + 40(40))/50 = 50.
That is the average of the two speeds. The correct relation gives dz/dt = 2500/50 = 50 mph.

derivatives-in-context__dc-differentials.prompt: A quantity s is measured with a 4% error. What is the error in √s?

options.label: About 2% — the exponent is 1/2, so the relative error is halved.
options.feedback: Right. Roots are forgiving: taking a square root of a noisy measurement quietens the noise.

options.label: Also 4%.
options.feedback: Only if the exponent were 1. Here it is 1/2, so the relative error is halved.

options.label: 8% — the error doubles.
options.feedback: Doubling happens when you SQUARE. A square root does the opposite.
That would be squaring the error itself, which is not what the rule says. Multiply the relative error by the EXPONENT, which is 1/2.

derivatives-in-context__dc-differentials.prompt: A cube's side is measured as 10 cm with an error of up to 0.1 cm. Estimate the resulting error in the VOLUME, in cm³.

numericErrors.feedback: That is the error in the SIDE. The derivative converts it: dV = 3s²·ds = 3(100)(0.1) = 30 cm³.
That is 3 × ds × 10 — a factor of s missing. dV = 3s²·ds = 300 × 0.1 = 30.
That is the volume itself, not the error in it.

derivatives-in-context__dc-differentials.explorationFeedback: Inspect the required exact-number states before checking.
derivatives-in-context__dc-differentials.fallbackFeedback: dV = 3s²·ds = 3(100)(0.1) = 30 cm³ — and the true change is 30.301.
derivatives-in-context__dc-differentials.successFeedback: dV = 3s²·ds = 3(100)(0.1) = 30 cm³ — and the true change is 30.301.

derivatives-in-context__dc-differentials.prompt: A circle's radius is measured with a 1% error. What is the resulting percentage error in the AREA?

approxConstants.label: the percentage error in the radius

numericErrors.feedback: The area depends on r SQUARED, so the relative error doubles: 2%.
The exponent is 2, not 4. dA/A = 2(dr/r) = 2%.
That is the rule for a CUBE (volume). An area goes with the square, so the factor is 2.

derivatives-in-context__dc-differentials.explorationFeedback: Inspect the required exact-number states before checking.

derivatives-in-context__dc-differentials.prompt: A cube's volume must be accurate to within 3%. How precisely must the 10 cm side be measured, in cm?

approxConstants.label: the allowed percentage error in volume

numericErrors.feedback: That is 3% of the SIDE. But the volume's error is THREE times the side's, so the side must be measured to 1%, i.e. 0.1 cm.
That is 3% written as a decimal, not a length. Apply it to s = 10 after dividing by the exponent 3.
That is 10% of the side — far too loose. It would give a 30% error in the volume.

derivatives-in-context__dc-differentials.explorationFeedback: Inspect the required exact-number states before checking.

derivatives-in-context__dc-distance__num.prompt: s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t on [0, 4], with v = 3(t − 1)(t − 3). Into how many LEGS must the journey be split?

commonErrors.feedback: The particle reverses TWICE (at t = 1 and t = 3), which cuts [0, 4] into three legs: [0,1], [1,3] and [3,4].
Only if it never turned round. But v changes sign at t = 1 and again at t = 3.
Two turning points make three legs, not four.

derivatives-in-context__dc-distance__num.fallbackFeedback: Turns at t = 1 and t = 3 → three legs.

derivatives-in-context__dc-distance__num.prompt: s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t. Find the DISPLACEMENT over [0, 4].

commonErrors.feedback: That is the TOTAL DISTANCE, which counts every leg. Displacement is just s(4) − s(0) = 4 − 0 = 4.
s(4) = 64 − 96 + 36 = 4, not 0. (s(3) = 0, but that is a different time.)
That is only the t³ term. Compute the whole thing: 64 − 96 + 36 = 4.

derivatives-in-context__dc-distance__num.prompt: The three legs run 0 → 4, then 4 → 0, then 0 → 4. Find the TOTAL DISTANCE travelled.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the DISPLACEMENT — where it ended up. The distance counts all three legs: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
That is only two legs. There are three: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
The legs cancel only if you add them with SIGNS, which is what displacement does. Distance adds their magnitudes: 12.

derivatives-in-context__dc-distance__num.fallbackFeedback: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 units travelled, though the displacement is only 4.

derivatives-in-context__dc-distance__num.prompt: s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t on [0, 2]. Find the TOTAL DISTANCE travelled.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the DISPLACEMENT, s(2) − s(0) = 2. The distance counts the backtracking: 4 forward then 2 back, so 6.
That is only the first leg (0 to 1). After the turn it slides back 2 more units, making 6 in total.
Check s(2) = 8 − 24 + 18 = 2. So the second leg is from 4 back to 2 — a distance of 2, not 6.

derivatives-in-context__dc-distance__num.fallbackFeedback: Legs: 0→4 (distance 4) and 4→2 (distance 2). Total = 6, though the displacement is only 2.

derivatives-in-context__dc-ladder__mcq.prompt: Differentiate x² + y² = 100 with respect to time.

options.label: 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt) = 0
options.feedback: Right. The 100 is a constant — the ladder never changes length — so the whole thing must balance to zero.

options.label: 2x + 2y = 0
options.feedback: Each variable owes a d/dt. Without them you have differentiated with respect to x and y, not with respect to time.

options.label: 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt) = 100
options.feedback: The 100 is a CONSTANT, and constants differentiate to 0. The ladder's length is not changing.

options.label: x² + y² = 0
options.feedback: Nothing has been differentiated at all — the d/dt has not been applied.

derivatives-in-context__dc-ladder__numer.prompt: The ladder is 10 ft long and its foot is 6 ft from the wall. How high is the top?

commonErrors.feedback: That is 10 − 6. Use Pythagoras: y² = 100 − 36 = 64, so y = 8.
That is the LADDER's length, which is the hypotenuse. The height is √(100 − 36) = 8.
That is the distance from the wall. The height is 8 — the 6-8-10 triangle.

derivatives-in-context__dc-ladder__numer.prompt: x = 6, y = 8, dx/dt = 2. Find dy/dt, in ft/s (include the sign).

commonErrors.feedback: The magnitude is right but the SIGN is wrong. dy/dt = −(x/y)(dx/dt) = −(6/8)(2) = −1.5: the top is going DOWN.
That is −(y/x)(dx/dt) = −(8/6)(2). The formula is −(x/y)(dx/dt) = −(6/8)(2) = −1.5.
That is dx/dt with a minus sign. Solve 24 + 16(dy/dt) = 0.

derivatives-in-context__dc-ladder__numer.prompt: Same ladder, same dx/dt = 2. Find dy/dt when x = 8, to three decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: That was the answer at x = 6. At x = 8 the height is only 6, so dy/dt = −(8/6)(2) ≈ −2.667: the top is falling FASTER.
The magnitude is right; the sign must be negative, because the top is descending.
That is −(x/y)(dx/dt) with the fraction inverted or the rate dropped. It is −(8/6)(2) ≈ −2.667.

derivatives-in-context__dc-ladder__numer.fallbackFeedback: y = 6, so dy/dt = −(8/6)(2) = −8/3 ≈ −2.667 ft/s — faster than before, with the foot moving at the same speed.

derivatives-in-context__dc-lhopital__mcq.prompt: lim(x→0) (x² + 1)/(x + 1). A student applies L'Hôpital and gets 2x/1 = 0. What went wrong?

options.label: The form is not indeterminate — substitution gives 1/1 = 1. L'Hôpital does not apply, and using it produced a wrong answer.
options.feedback: Right, and this is the whole reason the form must be checked FIRST. The rule gave a tidy, confident, wrong number.

options.label: They differentiated wrongly.
options.feedback: The derivatives are right: 2x and 1. The error is that the rule should never have been applied at all.

options.label: They should have used the quotient rule.
options.feedback: Neither the quotient rule nor any other differentiation is needed here. Substitute directly: (0 + 1)/(0 + 1) = 1, and the limit is done.

options.label: Nothing — 0 is correct.
options.feedback: Substitute directly: (0 + 1)/(0 + 1) = 1. The function is perfectly well-behaved at 0, and the answer is 1.

derivatives-in-context__dc-lhopital__num.prompt: lim(x→2) (x² − 4)/(x − 2). Apply L'Hôpital: differentiate top and bottom separately.

commonErrors.feedback: That is what you get by substituting x = 2 into the ORIGINAL — the 0/0 form. L'Hôpital says differentiate first: 2x/1 = 4.
That is x. The derivative of the top is 2x, which at x = 2 is 4.
That is the derivative of the BOTTOM alone. The rule takes the RATIO: 2x/1 = 4.

derivatives-in-context__dc-lhopital__num.fallbackFeedback: 0/0 → differentiate top and bottom: 2x/1 → 4. Exactly what cancelling gave.

commonErrors.feedback: That is what substitution gives — the 0/0 form. Differentiate: cos x / 1, which at 0 is 1.
That is the DEGREES answer. Calculus works in radians, where the limit is exactly 1.
The derivative of sin is +cos, with no minus sign. cos 0 = 1.

derivatives-in-context__dc-lhopital__num.prompt: lim(x→0) (1 − cos x)/x². Give a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is what one application leaves you looking at (sin x/(2x)) if you substitute too early. It is still 0/0 — apply the rule again: cos x/2 → 1/2.
That is the limit of sin x / x. Here there is an extra factor of 2 in the denominator: cos x / 2 → 1/2.
That is the reciprocal. The second application gives cos x / 2, which at 0 is 1/2.

derivatives-in-context__dc-linearisation.prompt: The error in a linear approximation grows like (x − a)². If you double the distance from a, roughly what happens to the error?

options.label: It quadruples.
options.feedback: Right — squaring the distance squares the error. Move twice as far and pay four times the price.

options.label: It doubles.
options.feedback: That would be a LINEAR error growth. The (x − a)² says the error is quadratic in the distance.

options.label: It stays the same.
options.feedback: The tangent and the curve diverge steadily. Distance is precisely what ruins the approximation.

options.label: It halves.
options.feedback: Errors do not shrink as you move AWAY from the point of tangency.

derivatives-in-context__dc-linearisation.prompt: Two curves are linearised at the same point. One has |f″| = 0.01, the other |f″| = 100. Which linearisation is trustworthy over a wider range?

options.label: The one with |f″| = 0.01 — it is nearly straight already.
options.feedback: Right. Curvature is exactly what makes a curve leave its tangent, and a curve that barely bends barely leaves.

options.label: The one with |f″| = 100.
options.feedback: That curve bends violently, so it peels away from the tangent almost immediately. Its linearisation is trustworthy only very close in.

options.label: They are equally trustworthy.
options.feedback: The error is proportional to |f″|. A hundred-fold difference in curvature is a hundred-fold difference in error.

options.label: Neither works at all.
options.feedback: Both work — near enough to a. The question is only how NEAR is near enough, and f″ answers it.

derivatives-in-context__dc-linearisation.prompt: Why can f(x) = |x| not be linearised at x = 0?

options.label: f′(0) does not exist — there is no tangent line, so there is nothing to build L(x) from.
options.feedback: Right. L(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a) needs f′(a), and at a corner that number does not exist.

options.label: Because |x| is not continuous there.
options.feedback: It is perfectly continuous. The failure is in the SLOPE, not the value — which is exactly the distinction C1 drew.

options.label: Because f(0) = 0.
options.feedback: A zero value causes no trouble at all. Plenty of functions are linearised at points where they vanish.

options.label: It can be — just use slope 0.
options.feedback: Averaging the two one-sided slopes is not something the definition permits, and the resulting line fits neither side of the corner.

derivatives-in-context__dc-linearisation.prompt: The linear estimate of √9.1 was out by about 0.00005. Roughly how many times bigger is the error for √10 (ten times further from a = 9)?

commonErrors.feedback: The error grows like the SQUARE of the distance. Ten times the distance means 10² = 100 times the error.
Doubling would be a linear error law. The (x − a)² makes it quadratic.
That would be a cubic law. The error goes like the square: 10² = 100.

derivatives-in-context__dc-linearisation.fallbackFeedback: Error ~ (x − a)², so 10× the distance gives 100× the error — about 0.005, and the true error is 0.0044.

derivatives-in-context__dc-linearisation.prompt: √x is concave down. Is the linear estimate of √9.1 too big or too small?

options.label: Too big — the tangent to a concave-down curve lies above it.
options.feedback: Right: 3.01667 versus a true 3.01662. You could predict the direction of the error without knowing the answer.

options.label: Too small.
options.feedback: That happens for a concave-UP curve, where the tangent sits underneath. √x bends the other way.

options.label: Exactly right.
options.feedback: A straight line cannot match a curve exactly, except at the point of tangency itself.

options.label: Impossible to tell without computing it.
options.feedback: The sign of f″ tells you, and it tells you in advance. That is what makes concavity useful rather than decorative.

derivatives-in-context__dc-linearisation.prompt: f(x) = √x. Find f′(9) as a decimal to three places.

commonErrors.feedback: That is f(9) = √9, the VALUE. Its slope there is 1/(2√9) = 1/6 ≈ 0.167.
That is the exponent 1/2. It must still multiply x^(−1/2) = 1/3.
That is 2√9. The derivative has it in the DENOMINATOR: 1/(2√x).

derivatives-in-context__dc-linearisation.prompt: Estimate √9.1 using L(x) = 3 + (1/6)(x − 9). Give four decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: That adds the whole 0.1 to 3. The tangent's slope is 1/6, so the RISE is only 0.1/6 ≈ 0.0167.
That is √9. The linearisation adds (1/6)(0.1) ≈ 0.0167 to it.

derivatives-in-context__dc-linearisation.prompt: Estimate 2.1³ using the tangent at x = 2.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the TRUE value. The linear estimate is L(2.1) = 8 + 12(0.1) = 9.2 — a little short, as concave-up guarantees.
That is f(2). The tangent adds 12 × 0.1 = 1.2 to it.
Check the increment: 12 × (2.1 − 2) = 12 × 0.1 = 1.2, not 12 × 2.1.

derivatives-in-context__dc-linearisation.fallbackFeedback: L(2.1) = 8 + 12(0.1) = 9.2, against a true 9.261 — an undershoot, as concave-up predicts.

derivatives-in-context__dc-motion__mcq.prompt: At t = 2: v = −3 and a = 0. What is the particle doing?

options.label: Moving backward at a steady speed, for that instant.
options.feedback: Right. Negative velocity means backward; zero acceleration means the velocity is momentarily not changing at all.

options.label: Stopped.
options.feedback: Stopped means v = 0. Here v = −3 — it is moving, just in the negative direction.

options.label: Slowing down.
options.feedback: Slowing down needs the SPEED to be falling, which needs v and a to have opposite signs. Here a = 0, so the speed is momentarily constant.

options.label: Speeding up.
options.feedback: With a = 0 the velocity is not changing at that instant, so the speed is not increasing either.

derivatives-in-context__dc-motion__numer.prompt: s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t. Find the acceleration at t = 1.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the VELOCITY at t = 1: v(1) = 3 − 12 + 9 = 0. The particle is momentarily at rest, but it is still accelerating: a(1) = 6 − 12 = −6.
That is the POSITION s(1) = 1 − 6 + 9 = 4. The acceleration is s″(1) = −6.
That is the coefficient in a = 6t − 12. Substitute t = 1: 6 − 12 = −6.

derivatives-in-context__dc-motion__numer.prompt: s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t, so v(t) = 3(t − 1)(t − 3). At how many instants is the particle at rest?

commonErrors.feedback: 3(t − 1)(t − 3) = 0 has TWO roots: t = 1 and t = 3. The particle stops at both.
The velocity certainly reaches zero — at t = 1 and t = 3.
A quadratic velocity has at most two zeros, and here it has exactly two.

derivatives-in-context__dc-motion__numer.fallbackFeedback: v = 3(t − 1)(t − 3) = 0 at t = 1 and t = 3: two instants of rest.

derivatives-in-context__dc-motion__numer.prompt: s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t. Where is the particle the FIRST time it comes to rest?

commonErrors.feedback: That is WHEN it stops (t = 1). The question asks WHERE: s(1) = 1 − 6 + 9 = 4.
That is s(3), the position at the SECOND stop. The first stop is at t = 1, where s = 4.
That is the second time it stops. The first is t = 1, and its position there is 4.

derivatives-in-context__dc-motion__numer.fallbackFeedback: v = 0 first at t = 1, and s(1) = 4.

derivatives-in-context__dc-other-forms__.prompt: Order these from SLOWEST-growing to FASTEST, as x → ∞.

misorderFeedback.feedback: eˣ is the fastest of the three. Apply L'Hôpital to x³/eˣ and watch the polynomial get ground down to nothing while eˣ survives untouched.
ln x is the slowest — it is beaten even by √x, let alone by x³.

derivatives-in-context__dc-other-forms__.missFeedback: ln x ≪ any power of x ≪ eˣ.
derivatives-in-context__dc-other-forms__.successFeedback: Logarithms crawl, powers walk, exponentials sprint — and L'Hôpital is what proves it.

derivatives-in-context__dc-other-forms__.prompt: lim(x→0⁺) x·ln x is the indeterminate form 0·(−∞). How do you make L'Hôpital applicable?

options.label: Rewrite as (ln x)/(1/x) — now it is −∞/∞, which the rule handles.
options.feedback: Right. Pushing one factor downstairs as its reciprocal turns a product into a quotient, and quotients are the rule's native language.

options.label: Apply L'Hôpital directly to the product.
options.feedback: The rule is stated for QUOTIENTS. There is no bottom to differentiate, so the move is not even defined.

options.label: The limit is 0, since one factor goes to 0.
options.feedback: That is precisely what 'indeterminate' rules out: zero times something unbounded can come out as anything. It must be resolved, not assumed.

options.label: The limit is −∞, since ln x → −∞.
options.feedback: The other factor is racing to zero at the same time, and which one wins is the entire question. (It is the x — the limit is 0.)

derivatives-in-context__dc-other-forms__.prompt: lim(x→∞) x/eˣ. Apply L'Hôpital and give the value.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the ratio of the leading coefficients, which is not how limits at infinity work here. After differentiating you have 1/eˣ, and eˣ runs away — so the limit is 0.
The limit is a specific number: 1/eˣ → 0 as x grows without bound.

derivatives-in-context__dc-other-forms__.prompt: lim(x→0⁺) x·ln x. Give the value.

commonErrors.feedback: Rewrite as (ln x)/(1/x) and apply the rule: it simplifies to −x, which goes to 0.
It does not run away to a negative value — the x crushes the logarithm, and the limit is exactly 0.

derivatives-in-context__dc-related-rates.prompt: A circle's area is A = πr². Differentiate with respect to TIME.

options.label: dA/dt = 2πr · (dr/dt)
options.feedback: Right — r depends on t, so the chain rule attaches dr/dt. That factor is the whole subject.

options.label: dA/dt = 2πr
options.feedback: That is dA/dr — the derivative with respect to the RADIUS. Differentiating with respect to time adds a factor of dr/dt.

options.label: dA/dt = πr²
options.feedback: That is the area itself, undifferentiated.

options.label: dA/dt = 2π
options.feedback: The r has vanished. d/dr[πr²] = 2πr, and then the chain rule multiplies by dr/dt.

derivatives-in-context__dc-related-rates.prompt: To find dA/dt when r = 3, a student writes A = π(3²) = 9π and then differentiates. What goes wrong?

options.label: 9π is a constant, so its derivative is 0 — the substitution destroyed the very change being measured.
options.feedback: Right. r = 3 is true at ONE INSTANT, not always. Differentiate with r general, and substitute only at the end.

options.label: Nothing — it is a valid shortcut.
options.feedback: It gives dA/dt = 0, which claims the circle is not growing at all. The substitution froze the radius.

options.label: The 9π should be 6π.
options.feedback: The arithmetic is fine: π(3)² = 9π. The error is doing it too EARLY.

options.label: π should be differentiated too.
options.feedback: π really is a constant, and its derivative really is zero. The problem is that r was treated like one.

derivatives-in-context__dc-related-rates.prompt: A circle's radius grows at dr/dt = 2 cm/s. Find dA/dt when r = 3, as a multiple of π (give just the number).

commonErrors.feedback: That is 2πr at r = 3 without the dr/dt = 2. The chain rule multiplies by the rate: 2π(3)(2) = 12π.
That is the AREA (9π), not its rate of change.
Check: dA/dt = 2πr·(dr/dt) = 2π(3)(2) = 12π.

derivatives-in-context__dc-related-rates.prompt: A spherical balloon's radius grows at 2 cm/s. Find dV/dt when r = 3, as a multiple of π (give just the number).

commonErrors.feedback: That is 4πr² at r = 3 without the dr/dt = 2. Multiply by the rate: 4π(9)(2) = 72π.
That is the volume-ish, not the rate. dV/dt = 4πr²·(dr/dt) = 72π.
Check the derivative: d/dr[(4/3)πr³] = 4πr², which is 36π at r = 3, and then × 2 = 72π.

derivatives-in-context__dc-speed__dragBu.prompt: In which cases is the particle SPEEDING UP?

items.label: v = 4, a = 3
items.feedback: Both positive: the push is in the direction of travel, so the speed grows.

items.label: v = 4, a = −3
items.feedback: Opposite signs: moving forward, being pushed backward. Braking.

items.label: v = −4, a = −3
items.feedback: Both negative: reversing, and being pushed further backward. The SPEED |v| is growing.

items.label: v = −4, a = 3
items.feedback: Opposite signs: reversing while being pushed forward. Slowing down (and about to turn round).

derivatives-in-context__dc-speed__dragBu.missFeedback: Compare the two SIGNS. Same means speeding up; opposite means slowing down.
derivatives-in-context__dc-speed__dragBu.successFeedback: Same sign, speeding up. Opposite sign, slowing down. The sign of a alone never decides.

derivatives-in-context__dc-speed__mcq.prompt: v = −5 and a = −2. Is the particle speeding up or slowing down?

options.label: Speeding up — both are negative, so the acceleration pushes it further in the direction it is already going.
options.feedback: Right. Its speed |v| = 5 is growing, even though its velocity is becoming MORE negative. Speed and velocity are different quantities.

options.label: Slowing down, because the acceleration is negative.
options.feedback: That is the classic error. Negative acceleration slows a FORWARD-moving object; it speeds up a backward-moving one.

options.label: Slowing down, because the velocity is negative.
options.feedback: The sign of v alone says nothing about speeding up. It is the COMPARISON of the two signs that decides.

options.label: Impossible to say.
options.feedback: The rule settles it: same signs means speeding up. Here both are negative.

derivatives-in-context__dc-speed__mcq.prompt: v = 3(t − 1)(t − 3) and a = 6t − 12. What is happening on the interval (1, 2)?

options.label: Moving backward and SPEEDING UP — v < 0 and a < 0, the same sign.
options.feedback: Right. It reversed at t = 1 and is now gathering speed backward. It will not begin to slow until a turns positive at t = 2.

options.label: Moving backward and slowing down.
options.feedback: That would need OPPOSITE signs. On (1, 2) both v and a are negative, so the speed is growing.

options.label: Moving forward and speeding up.
options.feedback: v = 3(t − 1)(t − 3) is NEGATIVE between 1 and 3 — the particle is going backward there.

options.label: At rest.
options.feedback: It is at rest only AT t = 1 and t = 3, not on the interval between them.

derivatives-in-context__dc-speed__numeri.prompt: v = 3(t − 1)(t − 3), a = 6t − 12, on [0, 4]. On how many intervals is the particle SPEEDING UP?

commonErrors.feedback: Check all four sub-intervals. The signs AGREE on (1, 2) — both negative — and again on (3, 4) — both positive.
On (0, 1) the signs are + and −, and on (2, 3) they are − and +. Both of those are slowing down.
Two of the four intervals have opposite signs, and those are the slowing-down ones.

derivatives-in-context__dc-speed__numeri.fallbackFeedback: Signs agree on (1, 2) [both −] and (3, 4) [both +]: two intervals of speeding up.

differential-equations__de-equilibrium__.prompt: Solutions near y = 4 move TOWARD it from both sides. Solutions near y = 0 move AWAY from it. What are these two equilibria?

options.label: y = 4 is stable (it attracts); y = 0 is unstable (it repels).
options.feedback: Right. A population near extinction grows away from zero; a population near the ceiling settles onto it. The field says so without a formula being written.

options.label: Both are stable.
options.feedback: Anything starting just above y = 0 grows AWAY from it. An equilibrium that repels is unstable — a pencil balanced on its point.

options.label: Both are unstable.
options.feedback: y = 4 attracts from both sides — start above and you fall to it, start below and you climb to it. That is the definition of stable.

options.label: y = 0 is stable; y = 4 is unstable.
options.feedback: Backwards. Look at the field: the arrows near 0 point AWAY from it, and the arrows near 4 point TOWARD it.

differential-equations__de-equilibrium__.prompt: dy/dt = 1.8y(1 − y/4). How many equilibrium solutions does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: A product is zero when EITHER factor is. y = 0 and y = 4 both make the right-hand side vanish.
The right-hand side certainly can be zero: at y = 0 and at y = 4.
That is the VALUE of one equilibrium, not the count. There are two: y = 0 and y = 4.

differential-equations__de-equilibrium__.fallbackFeedback: 1.8y(1 − y/4) = 0 → y = 0 or y = 4: two equilibria.

differential-equations__de-equilibrium__.prompt: dP/dt = 1.8P(1 − P/4). At what population is the growth RATE greatest?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the ceiling, where growth has stopped entirely — the rate there is ZERO. The fastest growth is at half of it.
An empty population does not grow at all. The rate is zero there too.
That is the rate constant k, not a population. The rate 1.8P(1 − P/4) is a downward parabola with roots 0 and 4, so it peaks at 2.

differential-equations__de-equilibrium__.fallbackFeedback: The rate is a downward parabola with roots at 0 and 4, so it peaks at the midpoint: P = 2 — half the carrying capacity.

differential-equations__de-equilibrium__.prompt: A population obeying dP/dt = 1.8P(1 − P/4) starts at P = 6. What does it settle on in the long run?

commonErrors.feedback: It does not stay put — 6 is above the ceiling, so the field points DOWNWARD there and the population falls.
It does not crash to zero. The field pushes it down only as far as the equilibrium at 4, where every segment is flat.
That is where growth is fastest, not where it ends up. The population settles at the ceiling, 4.

differential-equations__de-equilibrium__.fallbackFeedback: Above the ceiling the field points down, and the curve settles onto y = 4 — which it can never cross, because y = 4 is itself a solution.

differential-equations__de-euler__mcq.prompt: Euler gives 2.25 where the true answer is e ≈ 2.718. Why the undershoot?

options.label: y = eˣ is concave UP, so every tangent step lies below the curve.
options.feedback: Right — and it is the same f″ argument as C2's linearisation, applied once per step. The direction of the error was predictable before any arithmetic.

options.label: Because h is too big.
options.feedback: A big h makes the error LARGER, but it does not decide its SIGN. Even with a tiny h, Euler would still undershoot this curve — just by less.

options.label: Because e is irrational.
options.feedback: Irrationality has nothing to do with it. The undershoot comes from the geometry: tangents to a concave-up curve lie underneath it.

options.label: An arithmetic slip.
options.feedback: The arithmetic is right: 2.25 is exactly what two Euler steps of 0.5 produce. The gap is the method's error, not a mistake.

differential-equations__de-euler__numeri.prompt: dy/dx = y with y(0) = 1. Take ONE Euler step of size h = 0.5. What is the new y?

commonErrors.feedback: That is where you started. The step adds h × slope = 0.5 × 1 = 0.5.
That is the step SIZE, not the new value. Add it to the old y: 1 + 0.5 = 1.5.
That would be a step of h = 1. With h = 0.5 the increment is only 0.5.

differential-equations__de-euler__numeri.prompt: Continue: dy/dx = y, y(0) = 1, h = 0.5. After TWO steps (at x = 1), what is y?

commonErrors.feedback: That is 1 + 0.5 + 0.5 — using the same slope of 1 twice. The slope must be RE-READ at the new point, where it is 1.5.
That is after one step. Take a second: 1.5 + 0.5(1.5) = 2.25.
That is the TRUE value, e. Euler with h = 0.5 gives 2.25 — a noticeable undershoot.

differential-equations__de-euler__numeri.prompt: dy/dx = y, y(0) = 1, but now h = 0.25 (four steps to x = 1). Find y, to four decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the h = 0.5 answer. With four smaller steps you get (1.25)⁴ ≈ 2.4414 — closer to the truth.
That is the TRUE value. Euler still undershoots it, but by less than before: 2.4414.
That is after ONE step. Four steps give (1.25)⁴ ≈ 2.4414.

differential-equations__de-euler__numeri.fallbackFeedback: Each step multiplies by 1.25, so y = (1.25)⁴ ≈ 2.4414 — still short of e, but closer.

differential-equations__de-exponential__.prompt: A bacterial colony grows at a rate proportional to its size. Which equation says that?

options.label: dP/dt = kP
options.feedback: Right — and everything else follows. Twice as many bacteria means twice as many divisions per second, which is precisely proportionality.

options.label: dP/dt = k
options.feedback: That says it grows at a CONSTANT rate, however big it is — which would give a straight line, not exponential growth.

options.label: dP/dt = kt
options.feedback: That says the growth rate depends on the CLOCK, not on the population. A colony does not check the time before dividing.

options.label: P = ekt
options.feedback: That is (nearly) the SOLUTION. The question asks for the differential equation — the sentence about rates that produces it.

differential-equations__de-exponential__.prompt: Two samples of the same substance start with 1 kg and 1 microgram. Which halves faster?

options.label: Neither — the half-life is the same. The y₀ cancels: T = ln2/k.
options.feedback: Right, and it is why half-life is a property of the SUBSTANCE, not of the sample. The kilogram loses vastly more mass per second, but it takes the same time to lose half of itself.

options.label: The kilogram — it decays faster.
options.feedback: It loses more MASS per second, certainly. But it also has more to lose, and the two effects cancel exactly: the fraction lost per second is the same.

options.label: The microgram — less to get through.
options.feedback: It also decays proportionally more slowly in absolute terms. The PROPORTION lost per second is identical, which is what a half-life measures.

options.label: It depends on k.
options.feedback: k is a property of the substance and is the SAME for both samples. What the question asks is whether the starting amount matters — and it does not.

differential-equations__de-exponential__.prompt: A colony has dP/dt = 0.1P and P(0) = 200. Find P(10), to one decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the starting population. In 10 hours it has grown by a factor of e^(0.1×10) = e ≈ 2.718.
That would be 200 × 10 — LINEAR growth. Exponential growth multiplies by e^(kt), not by t.
That looks like 10% growth once. Exponential growth compounds continuously: 200e ≈ 543.7.

differential-equations__de-exponential__.prompt: A substance has a half-life of 5 days. Find its decay constant k, to four decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the HALF-LIFE itself. The constant is k = ln2/5 ≈ 0.1386.
That is 1/5. The relationship carries a logarithm: k = ln2/T ≈ 0.6931/5.
That is ln 2. You must still divide by the half-life, 5.

differential-equations__de-exponential__.fallbackFeedback: T = ln2/k → k = ln2/5 ≈ 0.1386 per day.

differential-equations__de-logistic__mcq.prompt: In dP/dt = kP(1 − P/K), what happens when P is very small compared with K?

options.label: The bracket is nearly 1, so dP/dt ≈ kP — it grows exponentially.
options.feedback: Right, and that is why the early stage of any logistic process looks exponential. The ceiling only makes itself felt as you approach it.

options.label: Growth stops.
options.feedback: Growth stops at the CEILING, not at the floor. A small population has plenty of room and grows nearly unchecked.

options.label: The population falls.
options.feedback: For 0 < P < K both factors are positive, so dP/dt > 0 — the population grows.

options.label: It grows linearly.
options.feedback: With the bracket close to 1, the equation is essentially dP/dt = kP — proportional growth, which is exponential, not linear.

differential-equations__de-logistic__mcq.prompt: A logistic population sits between K/2 and K. What is it doing?

options.label: Still growing, but ever more slowly — easing toward the ceiling.
options.feedback: Right: dP/dt is still positive but shrinking. Growing and slowing at once, which is the top half of the S.

options.label: Shrinking.
options.feedback: Below the ceiling both factors are positive, so the population is still growing. It only shrinks if it somehow overshoots K.

options.label: Growing faster and faster.
options.feedback: That is the BOTTOM half, below K/2. Past the inflection, the growth rate is falling.

options.label: Holding steady.
options.feedback: It holds steady only AT the ceiling. Between K/2 and K it is still climbing, just less and less eagerly.

differential-equations__de-logistic__num.prompt: dP/dt = 1.8P(1 − P/4). At what population is the growth rate FASTEST?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the ceiling, where growth has stopped completely. The fastest growth is at HALF of it.
An empty population grows at zero. The rate peaks in the middle: P = K/2 = 2.
That is the rate constant k, not a population. The rate is a downward parabola with roots 0 and 4, so it peaks at 2.

differential-equations__de-logistic__num.fallbackFeedback: The rate is a downward parabola with roots 0 and 4: it peaks at P = 2, exactly half the carrying capacity.

differential-equations__de-logistic__num.prompt: dP/dt = 0.3P(1 − P/500). At what population is growth fastest?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the carrying capacity K, where growth STOPS. The fastest growth is at K/2 = 250.
That is the rate constant k, not a population.
Half of the carrying capacity is 250, not 150. Read K from the bracket: 1 − P/500 = 0 gives K = 500.

differential-equations__de-logistic__num.fallbackFeedback: K = 500, so the growth rate peaks at K/2 = 250.

commonBuilds.feedback: You multiplied by y instead of dividing. The y is on the WRONG side of the fraction: dy/y = 2x dx.
That is true but not separated — the right-hand side still has a y in it, so you cannot integrate it with respect to x alone.

differential-equations__de-separable__bu.missFeedback: It can: the right-hand side is a function of x (2x) TIMES a function of y (y), which is exactly the condition for separability.
differential-equations__de-separable__bu.successFeedback: Right — divide by y and multiply by dx. Every y is now on the left and every x on the right, ready to integrate.

differential-equations__de-separable__mc.prompt: ln|y| = x² + C. Solve for y.

options.label: y = Ae^(x²), where A = e^C
options.feedback: Right — exponentiate both sides. The e^C is just another constant, so it is renamed A, and it can be found from the initial condition.

options.label: y = x² + C
options.feedback: That drops the logarithm. To undo ln you must EXPONENTIATE: y = e^(x² + C).

options.label: y = e^(x²) + C
options.feedback: e^(x² + C) is e^(x²)·e^C — a MULTIPLIER, not an addition. The exponent does not split into a sum outside.

options.label: y = ln(x² + C)
options.feedback: That applies ln to the wrong side. It is ln|y| that must be undone, and undoing it means exponentiating.

differential-equations__de-separable__mc.prompt: Separating dy/dx = 2xy required dividing by y. Which solution did that step lose?

options.label: y = 0 — the equilibrium. Both sides are zero there, so it IS a solution, but dividing by y excluded it.
options.feedback: Right. The general solution y = Ae^(x²) can never be zero, so y = 0 is not a member of that family — the algebra dropped it, and the slope field would not have.

options.label: None — the family covers everything.
options.feedback: y = Ae^(x²) is never zero for any A, so the constant zero solution is genuinely missing from it.

options.label: y = 1
options.feedback: y = 1 does not satisfy the equation: its derivative is 0 but 2xy = 2x, which is not zero. It is not a solution at all.

options.label: The negative solutions.
options.feedback: Those are covered — a negative A gives them. The one genuinely lost is y = 0.

differential-equations__de-separable__nu.prompt: dy/dx = 2xy with y(0) = 3, so y = 3e^(x²). Find y(1), to three decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: That is y(0), the starting value. At x = 1 the exponential has grown: y = 3e¹ ≈ 8.155.
That is e itself. You must still multiply by the constant A = 3.
That is 3², or 3e with e read as 3. e ≈ 2.71828, so 3e ≈ 8.155.

differential-equations__de-slope-field__.prompt: Match each equation to what its field looks like.

right.label: each COLUMN identical; steeper to the right
each ROW identical; steeper higher up

pairErrors.feedback: dy/dx = x depends on x, so it is the COLUMNS that are identical — the slope changes as you move right, not as you move up.
dy/dx = y depends on y, so it is the ROWS that match — the slope changes with HEIGHT.

differential-equations__de-slope-field__.missFeedback: Ask which variable the right-hand side mentions. That is the one the slope varies with.
differential-equations__de-slope-field__.successFeedback: Mentions neither → parallel. Mentions x → columns match. Mentions y → rows match. The field is a picture of the equation.

differential-equations__de-slope-field__.prompt: How many curves obey the instructions of a slope field?

options.label: Infinitely many — one through every starting point. The initial condition picks one.
options.feedback: Right, and that is the + C, drawn. The differential equation gives the FAMILY; the initial condition selects the member.

options.label: Exactly one.
options.feedback: Drag the starting value in the widget and a different curve appears each time. Every one of them obeys the same instructions.

options.label: None, until you solve it algebraically.
options.feedback: The curves exist whether or not you can write them down — the field defines them. Many differential equations have solutions that no formula can express.

options.label: Two — one going each way.
options.feedback: Each starting point gives one curve, traced both forward and backward. Different starting points give different curves.

differential-equations__de-slope-field__.prompt: For dy/dx = 0.5y, what happens to the field as you move upward (larger y)?

options.label: The segments get STEEPER — the bigger y is, the faster it grows.
options.feedback: Right, and that sentence IS exponential growth: the rate of growth is proportional to how much you already have.

options.label: They get flatter.
options.feedback: The slope is 0.5y, which grows WITH y. Bigger y, steeper segment.

options.label: Nothing changes.
options.feedback: That would be true if the equation mentioned only x. This one mentions y, so height matters.

options.label: They turn downward.
options.feedback: For positive y the slope 0.5y is positive, so the segments point up — and increasingly steeply.

differential-equations__de-slope-field__.prompt: For dy/dx = x, what is the slope of the field at the point (2, 7)?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the y-coordinate. The equation says dy/dx = x, and it never mentions y at all.
That is 7/2. The equation is not a ratio of the coordinates; it says the slope IS x.
That is xy. Read the equation literally: dy/dx = x.

differential-equations__de-slope-field__.fallbackFeedback: Read dy/dx = x literally: the slope equals the x-coordinate, so at x = 2 it is 2.
differential-equations__de-slope-field__.successFeedback: Right. Every segment in the column x = 2 has slope 2, which is exactly why the solutions are vertical shifts of one another.

integration-accumulation__in-accumulatio.prompt: In A(x) = ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt, what is t?

options.label: A dummy variable — it sweeps across the interval and then disappears.
options.feedback: Right. Rename it u and nothing changes. Only the endpoint x survives into the answer.

options.label: The same thing as x.
options.feedback: They cannot be: x is the fixed endpoint of the sweep while t is the thing doing the sweeping. Using one letter for both is a real error.

options.label: A constant.
options.feedback: t varies — it runs from 0 all the way to x. It is the variable being integrated.

options.label: The width of a strip.
options.feedback: That is dt. The t itself is the POSITION of the strip.

integration-accumulation__in-accumulatio.prompt: f(t) = 2t and A(x) = ∫₀ˣ 2t dt. Find A(3).

commonErrors.feedback: That is f(3) = 6 — the HEIGHT of the curve at x = 3, not the area under it up to there.
That is x itself. The area under 2t from 0 to 3 is the triangle (1/2)(3)(6) = 9.
That is base × height without the half. The region is a TRIANGLE: (1/2)(3)(6) = 9.

integration-accumulation__in-accumulatio.fallbackFeedback: A triangle of base 3 and height 6: A(3) = 9. (And indeed A(x) = x².)

commonErrors.feedback: That is the HEIGHT of f. The area up to x = 4 is a rectangle: 3 × 4 = 12.
That is the width. Multiply by the height 3.
That is 3 + 4. The area of a rectangle is height TIMES width.

integration-accumulation__in-accumulatio.fallbackFeedback: A rectangle of height 3 and width 4: A(4) = 12.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 5 − 3. You must accumulate FIRST: A(5) = 25 and A(3) = 9, so the difference is 16.
That is A(5) + A(3). The area from 3 to 5 is the bigger accumulation MINUS the smaller.
That is A(5) alone. Subtract A(3) = 9 to isolate the strip between 3 and 5.

integration-accumulation__in-accumulatio.fallbackFeedback: A(x) = x², so A(5) − A(3) = 25 − 9 = 16 — which is precisely the area from 3 to 5.

options.label: x⁴/4 + C
options.feedback: Right — and differentiating it back gives 4x³/4 = x³, which is the only check you ever need.

options.label: 3x² + C
options.feedback: That is the DERIVATIVE of x³. Integration runs the other way: raise the power, do not lower it.

options.label: x⁴ + C
options.feedback: Differentiate it back: (x⁴)′ = 4x³, which is four times too big. You must divide by the new power.

options.label: x⁴/3 + C
options.feedback: You divided by the OLD power. Divide by the new one: 4.

commonErrors.feedback: That is F(2) = 8 + 4 = 12 — you forgot to subtract F(1) = 2.
Check F: an antiderivative of 3x² is x³ (not 3x³/3 × 3), and of 2x is x². F(2) − F(1) = 12 − 2 = 10.
That is F(1). The answer is F(2) − F(1) = 12 − 2 = 10.

integration-accumulation__in-antiderivat.prompt: ∫₁³ (x³ + x)/x dx (for x ≠ 0). Give a decimal to three places.
